# GA-readiness assessment for Llama Stack

## Description

This epic resolves the strategy's gating unknown: no systematic GA-readiness
assessment of Llama Stack has been done, and the full inventory of gaps
between current Tech Preview quality and the GA bar is unknown. The epic
produces the definitive GA scope — a reviewed gap inventory covering API
stability, upgrade paths, scale limits, and error handling, with each gap
classified against the GA bar and a proposed remediation, sourced from TP
feedback scattered across support tickets plus engineering evaluation of the
current distribution.

## Scope

- Define the GA bar evaluation criteria for each category named by the
  strategy: API stability, upgrade paths, scale limits, error handling.
- Collect and consolidate TP feedback from support tickets and other feedback
  channels into a single deduplicated input set.
- Assess the current Llama Stack distribution (OpenAI-compatible REST API
  surface, LlamaStackDistribution CRD, provider plugin configuration,
  deployment and upgrade behavior) against each criterion.
- Produce a gap inventory: every gap listed with category, severity, evidence,
  and proposed remediation, forming the definitive GA scope for the
  graduation work.
- Identify which gaps belong to API stability and quality-hardening work
  streams so downstream implementation scope can be planned from the report.
- Publish the assessment report and obtain acceptance of it as the GA scope.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A GA-readiness assessment report exists that inventories gaps in all four
  categories (API stability, upgrade paths, scale limits, error handling)
  between current TP quality and the GA bar.
- Every gap in the inventory carries a category, severity, supporting
  evidence, and a proposed remediation; no gap is listed without a source.
- The report's gap inventory is accepted by the strategy stakeholders as the
  definitive GA scope for the graduation effort.
- The report explicitly partitions the gaps between API-stability work and
  general quality-hardening work so each downstream work stream can be scoped
  from it.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-1 (P0): the GA-readiness assessment that inventories the gaps and
  produces the definitive GA scope. This epic delivers the assessment itself;
  the remediation of the identified gaps is tracked separately.

# API stability guarantee for published Llama Stack surface

## Description

This epic puts a stability guarantee on the published Llama Stack API surface
so enterprise customers can build production GenAI applications against it:
versioned APIs, a documented deprecation policy, and a tested upgrade path
from the last two Tech Preview releases. Its detailed gap list is scoped by
the GA-readiness assessment.

## Scope

- Introduce API versioning on the published Llama Stack surface
  (OpenAI-compatible REST APIs and the LlamaStackDistribution CRD) per the
  versioning scheme the team selects.
- Document and implement a deprecation policy for the published API surface:
  how changes are signaled, how long deprecated surfaces remain available,
  and what guarantees GA customers get.
- Build and verify an upgrade path from the last two TP releases to the GA
  release, including upgrade procedures and validation that customer-relevant
  configuration survives the upgrade.
- Close the API-stability gaps identified by the GA-readiness assessment
  (specific compatibility breaks, undocumented surface, missing version
  semantics), or document an explicit waiver for each item not addressed.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The published API surface is versioned, and the versioning is visible to
  consumers of the REST APIs and the CRD.
- A deprecation policy is published and applies to the GA API surface.
- An upgrade from each of the last two TP releases to the GA release has been
  executed and verified by an automated or repeatable manual procedure, with
  results recorded.
- Every API-stability gap in the accepted GA scope is either remediated in
  this epic or carries a documented, stakeholder-accepted waiver.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-2 (P0): published API surface carries a stability guarantee — versioned
  APIs, deprecation policy, and a tested upgrade path from the last two TP
  releases.
- HLR-1 (P0, partial): closes the API-stability portion of the assessed gap
  inventory.

## Risks / Notes

- Detailed scope (which compatibility breaks must be fixed) is gated on the
  GA-readiness assessment outcome; the epic's shape above is stable but its
  work item list is rewritten from the assessment report.

# Remediate assessed GA-readiness gaps

## Description

This epic closes the quality gaps between Tech Preview quality and the GA bar
that the GA-readiness assessment inventories — error handling, scale limits,
and any other hardening items outside the API-stability work stream. Its
backlog is the remediation half of the assessment's accepted GA scope; until
that assessment lands, the size of this work is an estimate by the strategy's
own statement.

## Scope

- Remediate the error-handling gaps accepted in the GA scope: consistent,
  documented error behavior across the published surface instead of
  TP-tolerated inconsistency.
- Remediate the scale-limit gaps accepted in the GA scope: characterize,
  document, and where applicable enforce the supported scale limits of a
  Llama Stack distribution.
- Remediate every other assessed gap not owned by the API-stability work
  stream (operational behavior, resilience, configuration robustness), as
  enumerated in the accepted assessment report.
- Record a documented, stakeholder-accepted waiver for any accepted gap that
  will not be remediated before GA.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Every gap in the accepted GA scope that is not an API-stability item is
  either remediated or carries a documented, stakeholder-accepted waiver.
- Error-handling behavior on the published surface is consistent with the
  GA-bar criteria defined in the assessment.
- Supported scale limits are characterized and documented, and any enforcement
  the assessment calls for is implemented.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-1 (P0, remediation half): closing the quality gaps that TP status
  currently excuses, as inventoried by the GA-readiness assessment.

## Risks / Notes

- This epic's scope and size are unknown until the GA-readiness assessment
  resolves; the strategy's Open Questions table flags this explicitly. Re-plan
  the work item list from the assessment report before execution.

# Production support posture (SLOs, backport policy, config matrix)

## Description

This epic establishes the production support posture required for GA:
documented SLO targets, a backport policy, and a supported configuration
matrix that states which provider, runtime, and deployment configurations of
Llama Stack are supported at GA.

## Scope

- Define and document SLO targets for the supported GA distribution (for
  example availability and responsiveness objectives appropriate to a
  supported API layer), with the measurement approach for each target.
- Define and document the backport policy: which releases receive fixes, for
  how long, and how GA customers get critical fixes.
- Define the supported configuration matrix: the provider plugins (e.g.
  inference and vector providers), serving runtime pairings, and deployment
  configurations that are supported at GA, and mark everything outside it as
  unsupported.
- Validate the entries of the supported configuration matrix — each listed
  configuration is exercised and confirmed working, so the matrix reflects
  tested reality rather than intent.
- Publish the support posture documents where support and customers consume
  them.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Documented SLO targets exist for the GA distribution, each with a
  measurable definition.
- A backport policy is documented and covers the GA release line.
- A supported configuration matrix is published, and every entry in it has
  been validated by an executed test or documented verification run.
- No configuration is listed as supported without a corresponding validation
  record.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-3 (P0): production support posture is in place — documented SLO targets,
  backport policy, and supported configuration matrix.

## Risks / Notes

- Scale-limit findings from the GA-readiness assessment may refine the
  supported configuration matrix content (e.g. bounds on provider pairings);
  treat the assessment report as an input when it lands — the epic's
  deliverables and approach do not change.
- Ownership may extend beyond the component team (support organization,
  product management sign-off on SLO and backport commitments); the strategy
  provides no Impacted Teams table, so confirm stakeholders at kickoff.

# TrustyAI guardrails as supported Llama Stack integration

## Description

This epic promotes the TrustyAI safety-guardrails integration for Llama Stack
from an experimental flag to a supported, documented integration available in
GA distributions. After this epic, a GA Llama Stack distribution can use
TrustyAI guardrails as a first-class supported capability rather than a
Tech Preview opt-in.

## Scope

- Promote the TrustyAI guardrails integration for Llama Stack distributions
  out of its experimental/opt-in status: the integration works on GA
  distributions without an experimental flag.
- Harden the integration to supported quality: validated setup between a
  TrustyAI-managed service and a Llama Stack distribution's safety/guardrails
  surface, including the provider wiring on the Llama Stack side where the
  integration requires it.
- Verify the integration against the supported configuration matrix published
  by the production support posture work (documented SLOs, backport policy, and
  supported configuration matrix), so guardrails-enabled distributions are
  reflected as an entry in that validated matrix.
- Update integration tests to cover the guardrails path on GA distributions.

This epic is code-and-verification only. The customer-facing integration
documentation (what is supported, how to enable it, and its behavior) is
authored wholly in the GA documentation uplift work that runs after this epic,
not here.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A TrustyAI guardrails integration on a GA Llama Stack distribution works
  without any experimental or TP opt-in flag.
- The integration is covered by automated tests that run against the
  supported configuration, and they pass.
- Guardrails-enabled distributions are reflected as a supported configuration
  in the published, validated supported configuration matrix.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-4 (P1): safety guardrails via TrustyAI are a supported, documented
  integration (not an experimental flag) for GA distributions. This epic
  delivers the supported-integration code and verification; the
  customer-facing "documented" half of HLR-4 is delivered by the GA
  documentation uplift work (the TrustyAI guardrails integration guide).

## Risks / Notes

- The work spans the TrustyAI component and the Llama Stack distribution
  wiring; it is assigned to the TrustyAI team as the most relevant owner, with
  Llama Stack-side provider wiring in scope. The strategy provides no team
  table, so the two-team split (TrustyAI vs. RHOAI GenAI for the distribution
  wiring) must be confirmed at kickoff — if the Llama Stack-side wiring is
  substantial, split it into a separate epic owned by RHOAI GenAI at that
  point.
- The supported-configuration verification consumes the matrix published by
  the production support posture work; if that matrix slips, this epic's
  matrix-reflection acceptance criterion waits on it (hence the blocking
  dependency).

# Dashboard Llama Stack management on by default for entitled clusters

## Description

This epic makes Llama Stack management in the Dashboard a default-enabled
capability for entitled clusters, removing the Tech Preview opt-in gate. On
entitled clusters, users see Llama Stack management without any
configuration change; the capability remains available only where entitled.

## Scope

- Change the Dashboard's Llama Stack management enablement so it is on by
  default for entitled clusters, replacing the TP opt-in gate.
- Preserve entitlement behavior: clusters without the relevant entitlement do
  not get Llama Stack management surfaces.
- Remove or deprecate the now-obsolete TP opt-in flag and its configuration
  path, including migration handling for clusters that had explicitly opted
  in or out.
- Update Dashboard tests and feature-flag/configuration handling to cover the
  default-on behavior and the entitlement boundary.

## Acceptance Criteria

- On a cluster with the relevant entitlement, Llama Stack management
  surfaces in the Dashboard with no opt-in configuration.
- On a cluster without the entitlement, Llama Stack management surfaces do
  not appear.
- Existing opt-in/opt-out configuration is migrated or explicitly handled
  (no broken or silently ignored user settings).
- The enablement change can be reverted through configuration without code
  changes (rollback path for the default flip).
- Automated Dashboard tests cover the default-on and not-entitled cases and
  pass.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-5 (P1): the Dashboard enables Llama Stack management by default for
  entitled clusters (no TP opt-in gate).

## Risks / Notes

- This epic changes existing default behavior (replacing the opt-in gate), so
  the rollback-via-configuration acceptance criterion above is mandatory.

Write the values into `ai_signals`.\n183\t\n184\t| # | Signal | Frontmatter key | +1 Condition | -1 Condition |\n185\t|---|--------|----------------|-------------|-------------|\n186\t| 1 | Change specificity | `change_specificity` | Exact file paths, API endpoints, field names known | Vague scope (\"improve X\") |\n187\t| 2 | Pattern precedent | `pattern_precedent` | Similar changes exist in same codebase | No precedent in codebase |\n188\t| 3 | Adapter/plugin pattern | `adapter_pattern` | Follows existing reference implementation | N/A (0 if absent) |\n189\t| 4 | Existing foundation | `existing_foundation` | Extending existing code/feature | Greenfield, no foundation |\n190\t| 5 | Open questions | `open_questions` | All design decisions resolved for this epic | Open questions that would change implementation approach |\n191\t| 6 | External dependency | `external_dependency` | None | Upstream contribution or vendor coordination needed |\n192\t| 7 | Human process gates | `human_process_gates` | None | Requires human approval step |\n193\t| 8 | Repo access | `repo_access` | AI can clone and modify target repo | Repo inaccessible or special access required |\n194\t| 9 | Architecture claims | `architecture_claims` | Epic's scope or the strategy's premise about the component (surfaces, repos, deployment model, maturity state such as Tech Preview/GA) is corroborated by an architecture-context file — name that file in the rationale | Strategy asserts architecture that the context files contradict or cannot back |\n195\t\n196\t**Scoring `architecture_claims` (signal 9):** a strategy makes architecture claims whenever it states what a component IS — its maturity state (\"shipped as Tech Preview\", \"generally available\"), its CRD/API/repo surfaces, its deployment model — even when it never uses the word \"claim\".
